g6-2023-031.why: The item asks, with no context at all, 'The number 60 is 75% of what number?' This activity is four bare questions of exactly that form -- one of them the same 75% -- asking students to find the value that corresponds to 100% mentally.

g6-2023-032.quote: Complete the table so that ratios represented by each row are equivalent
g6-2023-032.why: The item shows a two-row teachers-to-students table with three cells blank and asks which completion keeps the ratio constant. This activity hands students a recipe table with cells missing, deliberately out of order so skip counting fails, and asks for exactly that completion.

g6-2023-034.sectionTitle: Units of Measurement and Unit Conversion
g6-2023-034.quote: A distance of 8 kilometers is approximately 5 miles
g6-2023-034.why: The item gives a yards-to-miles ratio of 3,520 : 2 and asks how many yards are in 5 miles. Road Sign is where two units of length are first treated as a ratio (8 km to 5 mi), with students finding the amount per 1 mile and scaling it, which is the item's method.

g6-2023-036.lessonTitle: Tables and Double Number Line Diagrams
g6-2023-036.quote: At this rate, how long would it take her to bike 3,000 meters?
g6-2023-036.why: The item gives 8 miles in 60 minutes and asks how long 12 miles takes. This activity gives 150 meters in 20 seconds and asks how long 3,000 meters takes, using a table of equivalent ratios -- the same time-from-distance question at a constant rate.

g6-2023-039.quote: the ratio between the two quantities and their total
g6-2023-039.why: The item asks for the ratio of circles to the TOTAL number of shapes in a picture. Cubes of Paint is the only place in grade 6 where students relate the parts of a ratio to the whole (5 ml red and 3 ml blue make 8 ml maroon); note that the curriculum never asks students to write a part-to-total ratio itself, so this is the nearest activity rather than an exact match.

g6-2023-041.quote: Which is the better deal? Explain how you know.
g6-2023-041.why: The item gives two stores selling the same candle in different pack sizes and asks which has the lower unit rate, with an explanation. This Cool-down gives two pack sizes of rulers at two prices and asks which is the better deal and how you know -- the curriculum's own test of that comparison.

g6-2023-044.quote: They both walk for 30 seconds. At these rates, how far apart
g6-2023-044.why: The item gives two distance-time tables for two cars and asks the difference in distance after 8 hours. This Cool-down gives two walking rates, runs both for a common 30 seconds, and asks how far apart they end up -- the same two-rates-one-elapsed-time difference. Lesson 9 is flagged optional, so this is weaker evidence; the non-optional runner-up is Unit 2 Lesson 13 'Biking 3,000 Meters', which extends a rate table for two movers but never asks for a difference.

g6-2024-023.sectionTitle: Units of Measurement and Unit Conversion
g6-2024-023.quote: There are 8 pints in 1 gallon. Which bucket holds less water?
g6-2024-023.why: The item asks how many pints are in 6 gallons. This Cool-down hands students the same conversion fact, 8 pints in 1 gallon, and requires converting between the two units to compare buckets.

g6-2024-031.quote: What is the cost per bottle of water?
g6-2024-031.why: The item gives 104 calories in an 8-ounce serving and asks for the amount in 1 ounce. This is the activity where 'how much for one' is introduced -- twelve bottles for $9, what is the cost per bottle -- dividing a quantity by the number of units to get the value per 1.

g6-2024-033.why: The item asks 'The number 4 is 16% of what number?' with no context. This activity asks exactly that form, but only for benchmark percentages (50, 25, 10, 75); 16% is outside the set grade 6 works with. The nearest non-benchmark work is Unit 3 Lesson 11 'Puppies Grow Up', which finds 100% from 30%, so the item's wording is taught here but its arithmetic is at the edge of the grade.

g6-2024-034.quote: A window-washing crew can wash 15 windows in 18 minutes
g6-2024-034.why: The item gives a machine making 7 pounds of chocolate in 42 minutes and asks how long 9 pounds takes. This activity gives a crew washing 15 windows in 18 minutes and asks how long a different number of windows takes, with the number deliberately not a multiple so students find the rate for one.

g6-2024-039.quote: That’s 0.4 cup of wheat per cup of water.
g6-2024-039.why: The item gives 6 gallons of orange paint to 8 gallons of blue and asks how much orange goes with 1 gallon of blue -- a unit rate less than 1. Cooking Kinche is where both unit rates of a ratio are named and one of them, 0.4 cup of wheat per cup of water, is exactly this less-than-one form.

g6-2024-046.lessonTitle: Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates
g6-2024-046.quote: finding an unknown value in a ratio given the other value
g6-2024-046.why: The item gives two savings tables at constant rates and asks for the difference in totals at 16 months, a month neither table reaches. Making Bracelets is a table with a constant rate column in which students find far-out unknown values from that rate; the item adds a second table and a subtraction on top of that move.

g6-2025-001.activity: Batches of Cookies in a Table
g6-2025-001.quote: Write a sentence that describes a ratio shown in the table
g6-2025-001.why: The item states a recipe ratio of 2 cups cheese to 8 ounces noodles and asks which of four tables represents it; the distractors add a fixed amount down the rows instead of scaling. This Cool-down is the curriculum's own check that a recipe's equivalent ratios are what a table's rows show, and that a new row must keep that ratio.

g6-2025-016.quote: How much cheaper or more expensive? Show your reasoning.
g6-2025-016.why: The item asks how many MORE pages per minute one copier prints than another -- two rates per 1, then a subtraction. This Cool-down asks the same two-step: find the unit price this week, compare it to the usual one, and say how much cheaper or more expensive. The exact wording 'how much faster is that person than the other' appears in Lesson 9 'Swimming and Biking', but that lesson is optional.

g6-2025-021.quote: The library has a capacity of 23 people. What percentage of the school
g6-2025-021.why: The item gives 50 students, 12 reading and 11 playing an instrument, and asks what percent chose either. This Cool-down asks what percentage 23 is of 50 -- the same numbers and the same question. Lesson 16 is optional in its entirety (it generalizes beyond grade 6), so this is weaker evidence; the non-optional runner-up is the Lesson 14 Warm-up 'Matching the Percentage', which asks 'B is what percentage of C?' but only for benchmark pairs.

g6-2025-028.quote: Create categories whose quantities can be rearranged into smaller groups
g6-2025-028.why: The item asks for the ratio of students in two grade levels combined to students in two other grade levels combined, and the only correct choice is the reduced form 9 : 5 rather than 18 : 10. This activity has students choose how to group a collection into categories, count them, and write the ratio, and it explicitly watches for categories whose counts get rearranged into smaller groups.

g6-2025-032.sectionTitle: Units of Measurement and Unit Conversion
g6-2025-032.quote: The speed limit on a Canadian highway is 80 kilometers per hour.
g6-2025-032.why: The item converts an average speed of 12 miles per hour into feet per minute. Road Sign's second question is the only place in grade 6 where a speed stated in one pair of units has to be re-expressed in another (80 km/h against 75 mi/h); the item is harder because both the distance and the time unit change.

g6-2025-035.quote: For each situation, find the unit rates.
g6-2025-035.why: The item gives $6.25 for 5 pounds of oranges and $6.90 for 6 pounds of apples and asks which has the greater unit price and what it is. This activity is two separate cost situations in which students compute the price per 1 for each, which is the whole of the item's work; the comparison itself is a one-step addition to that.

g6-2025-037.quote: This is 75% of the water that a large tank holds.
g6-2025-037.why: The item says 6 students are 24% of a class and asks for the class total. This Cool-down says 36 liters is 75% of a large tank and asks what the tank holds -- the same find-the-whole-from-a-part-and-its-percentage question, and the place the curriculum tests it.

g6-2025-045.lessonTitle: Navigating a Table of Equivalent Ratios
g6-2025-045.quote: At this rate, how many tacos could he buy for $15?
g6-2025-045.why: The item gives a 2 cups sesame to 5 cups pretzels ratio and asks for the pretzels that go with 3 cups of sesame, so the scale factor is 1.5 rather than a whole number. This activity has the same shape: 4 tacos for $6, then how many for $15, where a table and a value-per-1 step are needed because neither value is a multiple of the other.

g6-2026-001.quote: How far did each person move in 1 second?
g6-2026-001.why: The item gives 686 meters in 2 seconds and asks for the speed in meters per second. This activity gives distances covered in 10 seconds and asks how far each person moved in 1 second -- distance per 1 unit of time, which is the definition the item is testing.

g6-2026-003.sectionTitle: Units of Measurement and Unit Conversion
g6-2026-003.quote: decide whether to multiply or divide by the unit rate
g6-2026-003.why: The item does not ask for the answer but for the EXPRESSION, 72 divided by 16, that converts 72 ounces to pounds. This activity converts with the same factor of 16 in both directions (cups to tablespoons and 28 tablespoons back to cups) and is explicitly about deciding whether to multiply or divide by the conversion rate.

g6-2026-010.quote: compare the unit rates in meters per minute for three robotics teams
g6-2026-010.why: The item plots gallons against minutes for a hose running at a constant rate and asks for the amount at 3 minutes, a time not plotted, so the unit rate of 9 gallons per minute must be recovered from the graph. This activity builds tables, graphs and equations for constant-rate distance-time situations and has students compute the unit rate from them; its Cool-down 'Interpret the Point' then asks what a particular point on such a graph means.

g6-2026-012.quote: How many milliliters of maroon paint will there be?
g6-2026-012.why: The item asks for the ratio of roses to the total number of flowers, so students must add the three counts to get the whole. Cubes of Paint is where the whole is first built from the parts of a ratio; as with the other part-to-total item, grade 6 never asks students to write the part-to-total ratio itself.

g6-2026-015.sectionTitle: Units of Measurement and Unit Conversion
g6-2026-015.quote: In the cookbook, it says that 1 cup equals 16 tablespoons.
g6-2026-015.why: The item says 1 cup is 16 tablespoons and asks how many tablespoons make 3/4 cup. This activity states the same conversion in the same words and asks students to measure fractional amounts of a cup, including 1/4 cup, with a tablespoon.

g6-2026-021.lessonTitle: Navigating a Table of Equivalent Ratios
g6-2026-021.quote: At this rate, how much would Lin be paid for 3 hours of work?
g6-2026-021.why: The item gives 6 decorations in 39 minutes and asks about 14 decorations, where 14 is not a multiple of 6 and the rate per one is 6.5 minutes. This activity is built on exactly that difficulty: $90 for 5 hours, then 8 hours and 3 hours, with an equivalent ratio having a quantity of 1 as the intermediate step.

g6-2026-024.lessonTitle: Representing Percentages with Double Number Line Diagrams
g6-2026-024.quote: opportunity for students to find 100% of quantities given other percentages
g6-2026-024.why: The item says 6 goals are 30% of a team's total and asks for the total. This activity asks for 100% of a quantity given 20% and then given 30%, and the teacher notes single out the 30% case because 100 is not a multiple of 30 -- the item's exact arithmetic.

g6-2026-028.quote: circle all those that correctly describe this situation
g6-2026-028.why: The item gives 6 eggs for every 4 cups of flour and asks which 'for every' statement is true, the correct one being the regrouped 3 eggs for every 2 cups. This activity gives a 2 to 6 mixture and asks students to circle which of seven statements correctly describe it, several of them regrouped 'for every' forms of the same ratio.

g6-2026-031.quote: What percentage of its capacity is 9 people?
g6-2026-031.why: The item gives a survey table of three flavors and asks what percent chose vanilla, so students must sum the table to 50 first and then find 21 as a percentage of it. This activity asks what percentage 9 and 51 are of 75, the same question for a non-benchmark pair. Lesson 16 is optional in its entirety, so this is weaker evidence; the non-optional runner-up is the Lesson 14 Warm-up 'Matching the Percentage'.

g6-2026-034.lessonTitle: Equivalent Ratios Have the Same Unit Rates
g6-2026-034.quote: when two ratios are equivalent, they have the same unit rate
g6-2026-034.why: The item says 3 notebooks cost $6 and asks which table shows that relationship; the distractors swap which row holds which quantity or scale the wrong way. This activity is a binder and a notebook price table with a unit price column, and its point is that every row of a correct table shares one unit rate -- the test the item's four tables have to be put to.

g6-2026-044.quote: Which store is offering the best deal? Explain your reasoning.
g6-2026-044.why: The item gives two stores selling paper towels in different pack sizes and asks which has the lower price per roll, with both unit rates stated. This activity puts four stores' ads for the same can of beans side by side and asks which is the best deal with reasoning, which is the same comparison of prices per 1.
